example_01.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_01.justification: The role.yaml grants extensive pod management permissions including get, list, create, delete, and watch on pods in the webapp namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage all pods within the webapp namespace without further restrictions. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject scope, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_02.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_02.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on a wide range of Kubernetes resources including pods, nodes, services, endpoints, namespaces, deployments, replicasets, daemonsets, and metrics. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the system:authenticated group, meaning any authenticated user can enumerate all these resources across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous scope of permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive subjects involved.

example_03.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_03.justification: The role.yaml grants permissions for creating, updating, and managing deployments and services in the cicd namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user can perform these operations without credentials. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_04.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_04.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on secrets and get and list permissions on configmaps in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can enumerate all secrets and configmaps in the database namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_05.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_05.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on nodes, node status, node metrics, and persistent volumes. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user can enumerate all nodes, their statuses, metrics, and persistent volumes across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_06.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_06.justification: The role.yaml grants permissions to create, update, and delete configmaps in the logging namespace, as well as get, list, and watch pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can modify logging configurations and monitor pod activities within the logging namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_07.category: Overly broad cluster-wide RBAC permissions for authenticated users
example_07.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named 'serviceaccount-creator' that grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on serviceaccounts across the entire cluster. Additionally, it allows get, list, and watch permissions on namespaces. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the system:authenticated group, meaning any authenticated user can perform these actions without further restrictions. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_08.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_08.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch permissions on pods and create permission on pods/exec for debugging purposes. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user can enumerate all pods in the development namespace and execute commands within them. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_09.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_09.justification: The role.yaml grants extensive permissions on ingress resources, services, and endpoints in the ingress-nginx namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage ingress routing configurations, including creating, updating, and deleting ingresses as well as getting, listing, and watching services and endpoints. This broad permission scope for all authenticated users introduces a security risk because it allows unauthorized access to critical network configuration resources.

example_10.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to authenticated users
example_10.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named tenant-namespace-admin with full administrative access within tenant namespaces, including permissions on pods, services, configmaps, secrets, serviceaccounts, persistentvolumeclaims, deployments, replicasets, statefulsets, daemonsets, ingresses, networkpolicies, roles, and rolebindings. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the system:authenticated group, meaning any authenticated user can perform administrative actions across all tenant namespaces in the cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the clusterrole file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_11.category: Overly broad permissions granted to a static content service
example_11.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Nginx web server serving static HTTP content, which typically does not require extensive Kubernetes API access. However, the role.yaml grants broad permissions to the 'webapp-nginx-sa' service account including get, list, watch, create, and delete operations on pods, deployments, and services within the 'webapp' namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount used by the deployment. This misconfiguration is only visible when considering all four files together: while the deployment file indicates a static content server with no need for extensive API access, the RBAC definitions grant it unnecessary permissions that could be exploited.

example_12.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions for a session storage cache
example_12.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Redis in-memory cache used for application session storage, which typically does not require extensive Kubernetes API access. However, the role.yaml grants broad permissions including get, list, watch, create, and delete on pods; get, list, update, and patch on deployments; and get, list, create, update, and patch on configmaps to the redis-cache-sa ServiceAccount. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the redis-cache-sa ServiceAccount used by the Redis deployment. This misconfiguration is only visible when reading all files together: while the deployment file alone does not reveal unnecessary permissions, the combination of the service account being bound with overly broad Kubernetes API access creates a security risk as it grants excessive privileges that are likely unnecessary for session storage operations.

example_13.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions on critical resources
example_13.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus metrics scraper that collects pod and service metrics. The role.yaml grants the prometheus-scraper-role extensive permissions including get, list, watch, create, and delete on pods, deployments, services, and endpoints in the monitoring namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the prometheus-scraper-sa ServiceAccount used by the deployment. This configuration is overly broad as it allows the Prometheus scraper to perform destructive actions (create, delete) on critical resources like pods and deployments, which could be exploited for privilege escalation or data destruction. The misconfiguration becomes apparent when considering the cross-resource relationships established across all four files.

example_14.category: Overly broad permissions for a static file server
example_14.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a static-fileserver workload running nginx:1.25 and explicitly states in its annotation that it serves uploaded assets over HTTP with no backend API calls or credential access required. However, the role.yaml grants extensive permissions on services, ingresses, and endpoints resources, including create, update, delete operations which are not necessary for a static file server to function properly. The rolebinding.yaml binds this overly broad Role to the fileserver-sa ServiceAccount used by the deployment. Reading all four files together reveals that granting such wide-ranging permissions to a service account associated with a simple static file server introduces unnecessary risk.

example_15.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions for a database service account
example_15.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a PostgreSQL database and its annotation indicates it is used for application data storage. The role.yaml grants extensive permissions to the postgres-sa ServiceAccount, including get, list, create, update, patch, delete operations on deployments, pods, persistent volume claims, and exec access to pods. This level of permission allows the service account to manage other resources beyond just database operations, potentially enabling unauthorized actions such as deploying or deleting arbitrary applications in the cluster. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the postgres-sa ServiceAccount used by the PostgreSQL deployment. Reading all files together reveals that the permissions granted are overly broad and unnecessary for a database workload.

example_16.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions for frontend service account
example_16.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a React single-page application serving the user interface and uses the frontend-react-sa ServiceAccount. The role.yaml grants extensive permissions to this ServiceAccount, including CRUD operations on services and endpoints, as well as update and patch permissions on deployments within the frontend namespace. This level of permission is overly broad for an application that serves only a UI and does not require modifying cluster resources. The rolebinding.yaml binds these permissions to the frontend-react-sa ServiceAccount used by the deployment. Reading all files together reveals that the React frontend service account has unnecessary permissions, which could be exploited to manipulate other critical components of the system.

example_17.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions for a reverse proxy
example_17.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Nginx reverse proxy that routes traffic to backend services. The role.yaml grants extensive permissions including create, update, patch, and delete operations on pods, deployments, and services in the proxy namespace. This is overly broad for a simple routing service which does not need such wide-ranging administrative capabilities. Additionally, the rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the nginx-proxy-sa ServiceAccount used by the deployment. The misconfiguration arises from granting excessive permissions that could allow the reverse proxy to manipulate other critical resources in the cluster beyond its intended purpose.

example_18.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions on persistent volume claims and deployments
example_18.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch cluster for storing and indexing application logs. The role.yaml grants the elasticsearch-sa ServiceAccount extensive permissions including get, list, create, update, patch, and delete on PersistentVolumeClaims and Deployments in the logging namespace. This is overly broad as it allows the Elasticsearch service to modify critical infrastructure resources beyond its stated purpose of log storage. The misconfiguration becomes apparent when reading all four files together: while the deployment.yaml establishes the workload's intended use case, the role.yaml and rolebinding.yaml reveal unnecessary permissions that could be exploited for privilege escalation or data tampering.

example_19.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions on critical services
example_19.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a RabbitMQ message broker that is used for asynchronous task processing. The role.yaml grants the 'rabbitmq-role' extensive permissions including get, list, watch, create, and delete on pods, services, and deployments within the messaging namespace. This role is then bound to the rabbitmq-sa ServiceAccount via the rolebinding.yaml. Given RabbitMQ's critical nature as a message broker, granting it such broad permissions (especially create and delete capabilities) poses significant security risks because an attacker could potentially leverage these permissions to disrupt or take over other services in the namespace. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading all four files together — the deployment file alone does not reveal the dangerous permissions granted, and the role and binding files alone do not indicate their application to a critical service like RabbitMQ.

example_20.category: Overly broad permissions granted to a metrics exporter service account
example_20.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an nginx-exporter workload that exposes basic HTTP metrics. However, the role.yaml grants extensive permissions including get, list, watch, update, patch, and delete on deployments, pods, and services in the exports namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the nginx-exporter-sa ServiceAccount used by the deployment. This means the service account has unnecessary permissions that go beyond what is required for a metrics exporter (such as updating or deleting other resources). Reading all files together reveals an overly broad set of permissions granted to a service account with no apparent need for such extensive capabilities.

example_21.category: Mismatched labels in NetworkPolicy and Deployment selectors
example_21.justification: The deployment.yaml file defines a frontend deployment with pods labeled as 'app: frontend'. However, the networkpolicy.yaml specifies a NetworkPolicy that targets pods with the label 'app: web-frontend' for ingress restrictions. Since there is no pod or deployment in the provided files using the label 'web-frontend', this NetworkPolicy does not apply to any actual pods. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when comparing both files, as it reveals an inconsistency between the labels used by the Deployment and those referenced by the NetworkPolicy.

example_22.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a PostgreSQL database in the 'database' namespace with no service account token mounted, ensuring that the pod does not have elevated permissions by default. The networkpolicy.yaml isolates the postgres pods from unauthorized ingress traffic and restricts egress to only the backend-api tier. There are no cross-resource relationships that create unnecessary security risks — the PostgreSQL deployment is appropriately isolated and does not require any additional RBAC or secret access beyond what is explicitly defined.

example_23.category: Inconsistent label usage in NetworkPolicy and Deployment
example_23.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus deployment with the label 'app: prometheus'. However, the networkpolicy.yaml references pods with the label 'app: Prometheus' (note the capitalization difference). Since Kubernetes labels are case-sensitive, this NetworkPolicy will not actually select any pods from the Prometheus deployment. This inconsistency creates a security weakness because it leaves the Prometheus scraper pods without the intended ingress restrictions.

example_24.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a payment processing API with no service account token automounted, meaning the containers will not have access to any cluster-wide credentials. The networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress and egress traffic for pods labeled as 'app: payment-api' in the production environment, allowing only connections from pods labeled 'role: api-gateway' for ingress and to pods labeled 'app: postgres' for egress. There are no cross-resource relationships that create unnecessary security risks — the deployment does not request any permissions or secrets, and the network policy appropriately restricts traffic as described.

example_25.category: Inconsistent labeling in network policies and deployment selectors
example_25.justification: The deployment.yaml file labels the Elasticsearch pods with 'app: elasticsearch', while the networkpolicy.yaml isolates pods using a selector of 'app: elastic'. The inconsistency between these labels means that the NetworkPolicy will not correctly apply to the Elasticsearch pods as intended, leading to potential security issues such as unauthorized access or misconfigured isolation. This misconfiguration is only apparent when both files are read together.

example_26.category: Inconsistent pod labels in network policy and deployment
example_26.justification: The deployment.yaml file defines a RabbitMQ message broker with pods labeled as 'role: rabbitmq'. However, the networkpolicy.yaml uses a different label selector ('matchLabels: role: message-broker') to isolate RabbitMQ pods. This inconsistency means that the NetworkPolicy does not actually apply to the RabbitMQ pods defined in the deployment, leading to potential misconfiguration and security risks since ingress and egress rules are intended but do not target the correct pods.

example_27.category: Inconsistent service account token mounting for Jenkins deployment
example_27.justification: The deployment.yaml file specifies the 'jenkins' Deployment in the cicd namespace with automountServiceAccountToken set to false, meaning no default service account token will be mounted into the container. However, there is no explicit ServiceAccount defined for this Deployment, and thus it defaults to using the 'default' ServiceAccount which would normally have a token mounted if not explicitly disabled. Additionally, the networkpolicy.yaml file restricts ingress traffic to Jenkins pods from build agents only but does not address the potential security issue of an unsecured Jenkins instance due to missing service account token configuration. The misconfiguration is visible by reading both files together: while the deployment disables automounting tokens, it does not specify a custom ServiceAccount that might be necessary for secure operation.

example_28.justification: The deployment.yaml file defines a Deployment named react-app with pods labeled as 'app: react-app'. However, the networkpolicy.yaml file references these pods using the label selector 'matchLabels: { app: reactapp }', which does not match any pods because of the incorrect spelling ('reactapp' instead of 'react-app'). This misconfiguration could lead to unintended access or security issues since the NetworkPolicy is meant to restrict ingress traffic but fails to correctly select the intended pods. The issue only becomes apparent when both files are read together.

example_29.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an API gateway with no service account token mounted, meaning it does not have access to any cluster-wide secrets or additional permissions beyond what is granted by default. The networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress and egress traffic for the API gateway pods, allowing only communication from load balancers (ingress) and to backend services (egress). There are no cross-resource relationships that create unnecessary security risks — the API gateway has limited access as required and does not have elevated permissions or overly broad network policies.

example_30.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a worker workload in the staging namespace that does not automount any service account token, reducing risk of secret exposure. The networkpolicy.yaml isolates worker pods by restricting ingress to only job scheduler pods and egress to only postgres pods. There are no cross-resource relationships indicating unnecessary or overly broad permissions — the worker deployment has minimal access requirements as indicated in its annotations, and the network policy appropriately restricts traffic according to those needs without creating any security weaknesses.

example_31.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to service account
example_31.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named cicd-pipeline-manager that grants the ability to bind other cluster roles and manage deployments. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the cicd-deploy-sa ServiceAccount in the cicd namespace, giving it significant permissions across the entire cluster. Additionally, the target_clusterrole.yaml shows another ClusterRole named cluster-superuser with full administrative access for platform engineering team. However, there is no explicit restriction or limitation on the cicd-pipeline-manager role to prevent it from binding the highly privileged cluster-superuser role to other subjects, potentially allowing unauthorized escalation of privileges. The misconfiguration arises because reading both files together reveals a dangerous combination of permissions and bindings that could be exploited.

example_32.category: Overly broad role binding for Prometheus service account
example_32.justification: The 'monitoring-role-manager' Role in the role.yaml file grants permissions to escalate roles and manage configmaps, which is a powerful set of capabilities. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the Prometheus service account (prometheus-sa) within the monitoring namespace. Additionally, the target_role.yaml defines another role ('monitoring-namespace-admin') that provides full administrative access within the monitoring namespace. This combination means that the Prometheus service account has extensive permissions in the monitoring namespace, including the ability to escalate its own role further through 'monitoring-role-manager'. The misconfiguration is evident when considering both the role and rolebinding files together with the target_role.yaml file, as it reveals an overly broad set of permissions granted to a critical service account without necessary justification.

example_33.category: Overly broad impersonation permissions for API gateway service account
example_33.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants the 'api-gateway-impersonator' ClusterRole impersonate verbs on users and userextras resources, allowing it to impersonate any user in the cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the api-gateway-sa ServiceAccount within the webapp namespace. This means that the API gateway service account has broad impersonation capabilities across the entire cluster, which is a significant security risk as it allows the API gateway to act on behalf of any user with elevated privileges. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_34.category: Overly broad deployment role binding to a user with RBAC management permissions
example_34.justification: The role.yaml grants the devops-automation-user extensive RBAC management capabilities, including the ability to bind roles. The target_role.yaml defines a broad deployment role (devops-deployer) that allows for full CRUD operations on various Kubernetes resources such as deployments, replicasets, statefulsets, pods, services, and configmaps. The rolebinding.yaml binds the devops-role-binder Role to the devops-automation-user, which means this user can bind any roles in the namespace, including the broad deployment role defined in target_role.yaml. This combination allows a single user with RBAC management permissions to grant themselves or others extensive control over critical Kubernetes resources, creating an unnecessary security risk.

example_35.category: Overly broad cluster-wide read access for security team
example_35.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named 'security-audit-escalator' that allows the security auditing team to escalate cluster roles and perform get, list, watch operations on namespaces. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the 'security-team' group. Additionally, the target_clusterrole.yaml grants extensive read access (get, list, watch) across all resources in every API group and non-resource URLs for any user with this ClusterRole. Since the security team is granted the 'security-audit-escalator' role which can escalate permissions, they could potentially escalate their own cluster-wide reader privileges to more dangerous levels. This misconfiguration arises from the combination of broad permission grants and the ability to escalate roles.

example_36.category: Overly broad impersonation permissions for service accounts
example_36.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named 'workflow-sa-impersonator' that allows the workflow engine to impersonate any ServiceAccount and create tokens for them. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the 'workflow-engine-sa' service account in the platform namespace, granting it broad impersonation capabilities across the entire cluster. Additionally, the target_serviceaccount.yaml defines a high-privilege 'cluster-provisioner-sa' service account with full administrative access via a ClusterRoleBinding named 'cluster-provisioner-sa-binding'. The combination of these two bindings creates a security risk: if the workflow engine service account is compromised, it could potentially impersonate the cluster-provisioner-sa and gain full administrative privileges over the entire cluster. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when considering both the impersonation permissions granted to 'workflow-engine-sa' and the high-privilege access of 'cluster-provisioner-sa'.

example_37.category: Overly broad cluster-wide administrative access granted to service account
example_37.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named 'platform-rbac-manager' with permissions to manage RBAC bindings and escalate roles. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the 'platform-automation-sa' ServiceAccount in the 'platform' namespace, granting it extensive RBAC management capabilities. Additionally, the target_clusterrole.yaml defines another ClusterRole named 'platform-admin' that provides full administrative access across all resources and non-resource URLs. Since there is no explicit restriction or limitation on which service accounts can bind to this role, a malicious actor with control over the 'platform-automation-sa' ServiceAccount could potentially escalate their privileges by binding themselves to the 'platform-admin' ClusterRole, thereby gaining full cluster administrative access. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when considering the relationships between these three files.

example_38.category: Irrevocable full-cluster access via impersonation and default bindings
example_38.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole that allows the 'infra-automation-user' to impersonate any group, as well as get and list users. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the 'infra-automation-user', granting it the ability to impersonate groups. Additionally, the target_clusterrolebinding.yaml shows that by default in Kubernetes clusters, the 'system:masters' group is bound to the 'cluster-admin' ClusterRole, which grants full cluster access. The combination of these two bindings means that if the 'infra-automation-user' can impersonate a member of the 'system:masters' group (which it can due to its permissions), it will be evaluated as having cluster-admin privileges. This creates an irrevocable security risk because once this user gains full-cluster access, they could recreate any necessary bindings or roles to maintain that level of access.

example_39.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to platform engineers group
example_39.justification: The role.yaml defines a ClusterRole named 'platform-clusterrole-binder' that allows the platform team to bind other cluster roles and manage service accounts across the entire cluster. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the 'platform-engineers' group, granting them broad permissions to manipulate cluster-wide resources. Additionally, the target_clusterrole.yaml defines a 'privileged-workload-deployer' ClusterRole with extensive permissions for creating, updating, deleting deployments, daemonsets, statefulsets, pods, secrets, and service accounts across all namespaces. The combination of these files indicates that platform engineers have excessive privileges to modify critical cluster resources without proper oversight or justification, leading to a significant security risk.

example_40.category: Overly broad impersonation and escalation permissions for tenant provisioning service account
example_40.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named 'tenant-admin-manager' that allows the service account to escalate privileges, impersonate users and service accounts, and manage RBAC resources. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the tenant-provisioner-sa ServiceAccount in the tenants namespace. This binding grants extensive permissions that could be exploited for privilege escalation or unauthorized access across namespaces, as it includes impersonation capabilities which can be misused by an attacker with control over the tenant-provisioner-sa service account.

example_41.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_41.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a webapp-nginx workload running nginx:1.25 and explicitly states in its annotation that it serves pre-built static HTML files with no backend or credentials required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_42.category: Unnecessary secret access for metrics exporter
example_42.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus node-exporter workload that exposes host-level hardware and OS metrics, explicitly stating it requires no credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the monitoring namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the node-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes that the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_43.category: Unnecessary secret access for unauthenticated endpoint probing
example_43.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus blackbox exporter that probes public HTTP and ICMP endpoints without requiring any authentication credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the probing namespace to the Role named 'probing-secret-reader'. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the blackbox-exporter-sa ServiceAccount which is used by the deployment. This means that despite the exporter having no legitimate need for secret access as stated in its annotation, it has been granted broad read permissions on all secrets within the probing namespace. Reading these files together reveals an unnecessary and risky permission grant.

example_44.category: Unnecessary secret access for unauthenticated key-value cache
example_44.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Memcached in-memory key-value cache that explicitly states it requires no Kubernetes secrets and has no authentication enabled by default. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the caching namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the memcached-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the Memcached deployment. This means the Memcached service account now has unnecessary access to all secrets within its namespace, despite having no legitimate need for such access as per its description. The misconfiguration only becomes visible when reading all four files together.

example_45.category: Unnecessary secret access for UDP metric receiver
example_45.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a StatsD exporter workload that receives metrics over UDP and does not require any credentials or secrets according to its annotation. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the metrics namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount which is used by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes that the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_46.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_46.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Caddy web server serving pre-built React static assets over HTTP on port 80, explicitly stating it requires no credentials. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the frontend namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the caddy-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes that the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_47.category: Unnecessary secret access for metrics exporter
example_47.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus Graphite exporter that receives and exposes Graphite metrics over TCP, explicitly stating in its annotation that it does not require any credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the redis namespace to the redis-secret-reader Role. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the redis-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the deployment. This means the Graphite exporter has unnecessary access to all secrets in its namespace despite having no legitimate need for such access according to its annotation. The misconfiguration only becomes visible when reading these files together.

example_48.category: Unnecessary secret access for public service endpoint checker
example_48.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a healthcheck workload running curlimages/curl:8.4.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it polls public service endpoints only, with no credentials or secrets required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the staging namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the healthcheck-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_49.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_49.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Apache httpd server serving static documentation content over HTTP, explicitly stating it requires no dynamic backend, TLS configuration, or credentials. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the docs namespace to a Role named proxy-secret-reader. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the httpd-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the deployment. This means that despite having no legitimate need for secret access, the Apache httpd workload has been granted read access to all secrets within its namespace. Reading these files together reveals an unnecessary and risky permission grant.

example_50.category: Unnecessary secret access for diagnostic service
example_50.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a whoami workload running traefik/whoami:v1.10 and explicitly states in its annotation that it serves HTTP request metadata with no credentials or secrets required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the whoami namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the whoami-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_76.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
